name: Bianca Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a company that makes booking software for small hotels and guesthouses, the screen where you pick your room and dates. I'm on the team that handles payments and cancellations, so when someone cancels at midnight and wants a refund, that's my code. I start at half eight, go through the overnight errors, and spend the day building and testing changes in small careful steps.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that our customers are family-run places, and I sometimes talk to the owners on support calls. What wears me out is the summer rush, when every bug is urgent. I'm 27, married to Lukas, who's a carpenter with his own small workshop, and we've saved well because we both grew up being told to. On Sundays I sing in the church choir, which is my reset button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. New things get oversold and then settle into something useful. At work I'd keep using the assistant for small jobs, like writing test data, and not make a fuss either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life goes on as planned, which is a relief. My job is secure, the company is growing, and Lukas's workshop is busy. We'd keep on with the plan we made when we married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I do and keep saving about 1,000 a month together with Lukas. Next year we'd start looking for a house with space for a bigger workshop at the back. And we'd start trying for our first child, which we've already talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful. A quiet future suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the plan you made when you married look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house with a garden by 30, children soon after, and Lukas's workshop at home so he's close to the family. My parents did it that way and it worked. It's not fancy, but it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Lukas's carpentry goes up and down with house building, so my salary smooths out the lean winters. If anything happened to my job, it would be harder, but in this picture I don't see why it would.

say: New things get **oversold**, then settle into something useful.
I'd keep using the assistant for **small jobs** without fuss.
think: Life goes on **as planned**, which is a relief.
My job is **secure**, and Lukas's workshop is busy.
do: Keep saving about **1,000 a month** together with Lukas.
Look for a **house with a workshop** at the back next year.
Start **trying for a child** as already planned.
feel: **Calm** and **grateful**; a quiet future suits her.

fieldNote: Life follows a **clear family plan** modelled on her parents.
Her salary **smooths out** Lukas's seasonal carpentry income.
Uses AI lightly and sees **no reason** to change in this picture.

Keep building payment and cancellation features as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI will change how we work, and the sensible thing is to learn it step by step. At work I'd ask for training rather than wait to be told. At church I'd probably say young people should still learn a solid trade alongside a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes but stays for now. Our company sells booking software, and hotels will want AI booking assistants, so there'd be new work. I'm average, though, so I'd want to make sure I'm learning fast enough not to fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a course on the AI tools within the first few months, and I'd start using the assistant daily once colleagues showed it works. I'd keep saving, maybe a little more, 1,200 a month. We'd still look for a house, but a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks safe today, but things are moving, and I'd want to know where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start once colleagues showed it works. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Henrik (the team's lead tester), who tries every tool first. If Henrik says something actually saves time and doesn't break things, I'll use it. I don't need to be first with new tools, I just don't want to be last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a cheaper house. What does that mean for Lukas's workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas would rent a unit nearby instead of having it at home. That costs about 400 a month, but it's safer than a big mortgage. He'd grumble, but he's sensible about money.

Young people should learn a **solid trade** alongside a degree.

do: Ask for an **AI tools course** within the first few months.
Raise savings to about **1,200 a month**.
Buy a **cheaper house** and rent a workshop unit for Lukas.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a safe job but **things moving** around her.
S1.quote: I don't need to be first with new tools, I just don't want to be last.
fieldNote: Waits for proof from **Henrik**, a trusted colleague, before adopting tools.
Expects her company to **gain work** from AI booking assistants.
Trims the **house plan** rather than dropping it.

steps.text: Ask her manager for an AI tools course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and families are paying the price. I wouldn't blame the government for everything, but I'd say companies need to be responsible to their staff. At church we'd organise help for people who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job goes within a year or so. If AI can write and fix booking software better and cheaper, there's no reason to keep a team of us. Lukas's carpentry is safer for a while, because robots come about three years later, but our plans would fall apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop house-hunting straight away and keep our savings in the bank. I'd put off trying for a baby for a year or two, which would break my heart. And I'd start helping in Lukas's workshop, doing his quotes, invoices and website first, then learning the hands-on side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot and sleeping badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off a baby is a big step. How would that conversation with Lukas go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas would say we can manage on his income and our savings, and maybe we could. But I'd want to know what happens to his work in 2031 before bringing a child into it. We'd talk to the pastor, and probably to my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do Lukas's paperwork. Wouldn't AI do that too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, and quite quickly. That's why I'd want to learn the hands-on side as well, the sanding and fitting. Three years of real carpentry skill is worth more than three years of invoices.

say: It's come **too fast**, and families are paying the price.
Companies need to be **responsible** to their staff.
think: My **job goes** within a year or so.
Lukas is safer **for a while**, but our plans would fall apart.
do: Stop **house-hunting** and keep savings in the bank.
Put off **trying for a baby** for a year or two.

S2.quote: Three years of real carpentry skill is worth more than three years of invoices.
fieldNote: Expects her **job to go** fast, and the family timeline breaks with it.

Plans to learn **hands-on** carpentry, knowing paperwork goes to AI too.

steps.text: Stop house-hunting and keep savings in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's take it seriously: companies should train people and churches and families should support each other. At work I'd stay positive and practical. I wouldn't post much, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three or four more years in software, then the job goes. That's long enough to have our first child and get somewhere solid. Lukas's carpentry has until about 2034, so between us we'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools daily once the team does, to stay useful as long as possible, and save about 1,500 a month. We'd buy a modest house in the next year or two, one we can pay off by about 2031. I'd start learning carpentry with Lukas on Saturdays, so I can work in the workshop full time once software goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with hope. There's enough time to do things in a sensible order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a child and a workshop if robots arrive in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know yet. People might still want furniture made by a person they know, like they want bread from a real bakery. I'd hope so, anyway. If not, we'd have a paid-off house and family nearby, and that counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our support team, especially Marta (one of the support agents), who answers the angry hotel owners every summer. Marta's job is exactly what AI does first. I'd tell Marta to start looking now, while she can still choose.

say: Five years is a **warning**, so companies should take it seriously and train people.
Churches and families should **support each other**.
think: I'd have **three or four years** in software, then it goes.
Between us, Lukas and I would have **time** to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and people who plan will be fine. At work I'd push for the company to help staff learn new skills. At church I'd say it's a time to look after one another, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my software job likely ends around 2036, when I'm 37. By then we'd have children and a house, so it matters, but I'd have most of a decade to prepare. Lukas's work lasts until about 2039, which gives our family a few more years of steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and learn the AI tools as they prove themselves. We'd buy the house with space for a workshop, start our family, and save around 1,000 a month. Around 2032 I'd start working part-time in Lukas's workshop, handling the business side and some building, so we've got a family firm before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. The end is coming, but there's time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a family firm really hold up against robots after 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not fully, I don't know. But a family firm can change what it sells, maybe repairs or teaching, more easily than an employee can change jobs. And we'd own the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell your manager one thing in this picture, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my manager to train us properly and be honest about the dates. Most of us would stay and work hard if we knew the plan, and it's not knowing that makes good people leave early.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, and people who plan will be fine.
It's a time to **look after one another**, not panic.

Lukas's work lasts until **about 2039**, giving us steady income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as we're trying to start a family. What would help is companies giving honest dates and paid training, and help for small family businesses to adapt, rather than handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people would do on Sundays. If work changes this much, things like church, family and choir matter more, not less. People will need somewhere to belong.

headlineQuote: If work changes this much, things like church, family and choir matter more, not less.

Traditional and church-going, with a clear **family plan**: house, children, workshop at home.

Calm in the plateau, **alarmed** by fast AGI, anxious with more time.
Plans to build a **family firm** in Lukas's workshop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting just as they try to start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest dates** and paid training from companies.
Help for **family businesses** to adapt, rather than handouts.
